title: Modulation of neurogenesis by PDE inhibition

report.headline: Dead patent with a future (96/100, high confidence): a lapsed brain-cell-growth drug combo in a field that is still busy, but the road to market runs through the FDA and well-funded rivals.
report.what_it_is: This patent covered a mix of two drugs, rolipram (a PDE4 inhibitor) and buspirone, at doses meant to work better together at growing new nerve cells. The goal was to treat brain and nerve conditions by boosting neurogenesis, the formation of new nerve cells.

why_it_died.text: The owner, Braincells Inc, appears never to have paid the first maintenance fee, which is due 3.5 years after grant. The patent lapsed in July 2015 and gave up about 14 years of remaining term. The owner was a small entity. The record shows that the fee went unpaid, not why. Money or a change in priorities is a plausible reason, but that is an inference. No reinstatement has been recorded since.

case_for.point: The field is clearly alive. Several companies and groups are running Phase 2 trials of PDE4 inhibitors for cognition, schizophrenia, Fragile X and early Alzheimer's.
Others keep building on this idea. 26 unrelated filings citing it came after it lapsed, and 13 have priority dates from 2019 on. That drives the full marks for momentum.
Examiners saw it as relevant prior art. They cited it against 31 later applications, which suggests the core idea mattered to the field.
The main claim is short (17 words) and the family was filed in 6 jurisdictions. That shows the owner once valued it, and it scored full marks for breadth.

case_against.point: Interest here is clinical, not commercial. The evidence shows trials and designations, not revenue. Large players like Shionogi are already well ahead.
Some of the 'momentum' may be noise. The top recent citer, Augmedics, filed 9 of the citing documents, and those may not be about drugs at all. That is worth checking before you trust the signal.
Any drug needs FDA approval before it can be sold. That means years of trials and large costs, far beyond a typical startup budget.
The patent describes the idea, not how to make and dose it well. You would likely need to rebuild the process know-how yourself.

blockers.point: FDA approval (an NDA) is needed before sale. Regulatory exclusivity held by others can block you even where patents have expired.
22 later patents by other owners were cited against this one and may still be in force. They could cover nearby compositions or uses.
The original owner filed 2 later patents that cite this one and may still be in force, for example one on biguanides and GSK3-beta agents.
Well-funded rivals with active PDE4 programs may hold their own rights and have a big head start. This is why 'Clear path' scored only 6 of 10.
Manufacturing and formulation know-how is not in the patent and would need to be rebuilt.

assumption_to_test.assumption: A partner, licensee or CNS-focused investor would fund trials of an older two-drug PDE4 combo, even though rivals are already in Phase 2 with newer PDE4 drugs.
assumption_to_test.why_riskiest: A startup cannot pay for FDA trials alone. If no one with money sees an edge for this combo over the PDE4 programs already running, there is no business, however good the score.
assumption_to_test.how_to_test: In two weeks, for close to $0: (1) Search ClinicalTrials.gov and recent literature for any PDE4 inhibitor plus buspirone combination work, and note who is doing it. (2) Send short, non-confidential one-page pitches to 15-20 business development leads at CNS pharma companies and CNS-focused VCs or patient foundations, such as Fragile X groups. Ask one question: 'Would a synergistic PDE4 plus buspirone combo for neurogenesis be worth a 30-minute call?' Aim for at least 3 serious replies before going further.

attorney_questions: Do any of the 22 later patents cited against this one, or the owner's 2 later citing patents, appear to cover rolipram-buspirone or similar PDE4 combination compositions or uses, and are they still in force?
Could existing or pending FDA regulatory exclusivities on PDE4 inhibitors or buspirone affect the timing of a combination product?
Given that the lapse appears final with no reinstatement on record, what would a full freedom-to-operate review in the US and the other 5 family jurisdictions cost and cover?
report.disclaimer: Research and triage only, not legal advice. This report is not a patentability, validity or freedom-to-operate opinion. Patent status shown here comes from public records that can lag or be wrong. An expired patent is not the same as free to use: follow-on patents, regulatory exclusivity, trade secrets and standards can still block a product. Confirm with a registered patent attorney before acting.

signals.signal: PDE inhibition for CNS indications is being actively developed in the clinic, with multiple PDE4 programs in Phase 2 for cognitive and neurodevelopmental conditions.
Technical interest in the patent continued well after it lapsed, with many later filings by unrelated owners and steady recent citation activity.
Some of the recent citation volume may not reflect neurogenesis drug interest. Augmedics, a heavy recent citer, appears in the evidence only as a filer, and no evidence ties it to PDE pharmacology.
The original owner let the patent lapse early as a small entity, giving up about 14 years of term. This suggests it was not commercialized by that owner.

read.who_is_active: Alto Neuroscience (ALTO-101), Shionogi (zatolmilast, following its Tetra acquisition) and Healx are active per the evidence, and academic groups such as the University of Central Florida and the ROMEMA trial investigators are also involved.
read.market_read: PDE4 inhibition for cognition and neurodevelopmental disorders is a live clinical field with Phase 2 activity and regulatory designations, though the evidence shows technical and clinical interest rather than revenue. A founder entering this space would face well-resourced incumbents and should commission a professional freedom-to-operate review, since later filings and active programs may carry their own rights.

web.finding: Alto Neuroscience has started a Phase 2 placebo-controlled study of ALTO-101, a transdermal PDE4 inhibitor, for cognitive impairment associated with schizophrenia.
Shionogi, which acquired Tetra in 2020, received FDA Rare Pediatric Disease designation for zatolmilast, an investigational treatment for Fragile X syndrome.
The FRAXA Research Foundation reported positive Phase II results for zatolmilast, a PDE4D inhibitor, in Fragile X syndrome.
The ROMEMA Phase II proof-of-concept trial is testing the PDE4 inhibitor roflumilast in patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild Alzheimer's dementia.
